title: Three-Point Crosses: Gene Order and Double Crossovers

generated.pipeline: extract → Sonnet draft → Sonnet accuracy gate (separate agent) → Sonnet fixes

cards.front: In meiosis, what does a crossover exchange, and between which chromatids?
cards.back: Segments of DNA, between two non-sister chromatids.
cards.quote: A crossover exchanges segments between two non-sister chromatids in meiosis

cards.front: In a test cross, why can each offspring's phenotype be read as one gamete from the heterozygous parent?
cards.back: The other parent is homozygous recessive at every locus, so it contributes only recessive alleles and the offspring's phenotype shows which alleles the heterozygote's gamete carried.
cards.quote: so each offspring's phenotype reads one gamete from the other parent

cards.front: In a three-point test cross, what is the one idea that a middle marker adds over a two-gene count?
cards.back: A middle marker makes double crossovers visible; comparing observed and expected doubles reveals crossover spacing.
cards.quote: A middle marker makes double crossovers visible; comparing observed and expected doubles reveals crossover spacing.

cards.front: In a three-point test cross of linked genes, how many offspring classes are scored, and how do they pair up?
cards.back: Eight classes, in four reciprocal pairs: parentals, singles in the first interval, singles in the second interval, and doubles.
cards.quote: parentals (no detected crossover), single crossovers in each interval, and double crossovers (one in each interval, usually smallest)
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: In a three-point test cross, why are double crossovers usually the smallest classes?
cards.back: A double needs a crossover in both intervals. Under independence its probability is the product of the two interval probabilities, and the product of two small fractions is smaller still.
cards.quote: Under independence, a double's probability is the product of the two interval probabilities (probability and crosses), and the product of two small fractions is smaller still.
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: In a three-point test cross, how do you identify the parental classes and the phase of the heterozygous parent?
cards.back: Assuming every class survives and is scored equally well, the two largest classes are the parentals. They match the heterozygote's two chromosomes, so they show which alleles lie together on each chromosome (the phase).
cards.quote: The two largest classes, p q r and + + +, match the female's two chromosomes.
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: In a three-point cross, the alleles together on each chromosome of the heterozygote are called its {{c1::phase}}.
cards.quote: her phase, the alleles together on each chromosome, is known
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: A test cross of a p q r / + + + female gives parentals p q r and + + +. The two rarest classes are + q r and p + +. Which gene is in the middle?
cards.back: p. Each rare class differs from its closest parental only at p, so p is the middle gene and the order is q–p–r.
cards.why: The gene that switches in the doubles is the middle one.
cards.quote: So p is in the middle, giving q–p–r.
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: In a three-point cross, why is the gene in the middle of an alphabetical listing not necessarily the middle gene on the chromosome?
cards.back: Classes are listed in any convenient order, such as alphabetical. Map order comes from comparing the double-crossover classes to the parentals.
cards.quote: The alphabetical middle, q, is an outer gene.
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: A test cross of an A b C / a B c female (A, B, C linked) gives parentals A b C and a B c. The two smallest classes are A B C and a b c. Which gene is in the middle?
cards.back: B. A B C differs from the parental A b C only at B, and a b c differs from a B c only at B. So the order is A–B–C.
cards.why: The gene that differs between doubles and parentals is the middle gene.
cards.quote: So p is in the middle, giving q–p–r.
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: After finding the middle gene, how should every class be rewritten before counting crossovers, and what does each class show?
cards.back: Rewrite each class in map order and note where it switches from one parental pattern to the other. A switch in one interval is a single crossover; switches in both intervals mark a double.
cards.quote: Step 2: rewrite every class in map order, q to p to r, and note where each switches from one parental pattern to the other.
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: In a three-point cross, why is picking the smallest reciprocal pair as the doubles a reasoned choice rather than proof?
cards.back: A class can be small because its offspring survive poorly. The map-order sort labels the singles but cannot confirm which pair is the doubles; if survival or scoring may differ, independent evidence is needed.
cards.quote: Rarity is a clue, not proof: a class can be small because its offspring survive poorly
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: Map distance is measured in {{c1::centimorgans}} (cM), a frequency, not a length.
cards.quote: Map distance is measured in centimorgans (cM), a frequency, not a length: for a short interval, 1 cM means about 1 gamete in 100 is recombinant.
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: For a short interval, what does 1 cM mean?
cards.back: About 1 gamete in 100 is recombinant for that interval.
cards.quote: for a short interval, 1 cM means about 1 gamete in 100 is recombinant
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: Why must double crossovers be counted in both intervals when finding the map distance of each adjacent interval?
cards.back: A double includes one crossover in each interval. The formula is 100 × (single crossovers in the interval + double crossovers) / total.
cards.quote: Count every double in both intervals: distance (cM) = 100 × (single crossovers in the interval + double crossovers) / total
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: In a test cross with order X–Y–Z and 1,000 progeny, the single crossovers are 82 + 78 in X–Y and 94 + 96 in Y–Z, and the doubles are 10 + 6. What are the X–Y, Y–Z and X–Z map distances?
cards.quote: Count every double in both intervals: distance (cM) = 100 × (single crossovers in the interval + double crossovers) / total
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: In an X–Y–Z cross with 160 single crossovers in X–Y, 190 in Y–Z, 16 doubles and 1,000 progeny, what recombinant percentage results if Y is ignored and only X and Z are scored? Does it equal the 38.2 cM map sum?
cards.back: No: 35.0%. Doubles carry parental X–Z combinations, so only the 350 singles count. The shortfall of 3.2 points is the 16 doubles counted once in each interval.
cards.why: The two-point count misses double crossovers.
cards.quote: The doubles q + r and + p + carry parental q–r combinations, so only the 296 single crossovers count: 296 / 1,000 = 29.6%.
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: Why is even a three-point map distance a lower bound on the true amount of crossing over?
cards.back: Two crossovers inside one interval, with no marker between them, still escape detection, so shorter adjacent intervals give better maps.
cards.quote: Even 32.0 cM is a lower bound: two crossovers inside q–p or inside p–r, with no marker between them, still escape detection.
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: In a three-point test cross, what limits the method even with three markers?
cards.back: An even number of crossovers within one interval gives parental-looking gametes and goes undetected. Unequal survival can also upset the size ranking of the classes.
cards.quote: Unequal survival can upset the usual size ranking, and even three markers miss an even number of crossovers within one interval.

cards.front: The coefficient of coincidence is observed doubles divided by the number {{c1::expected under independence}}.
cards.quote: coefficient of coincidence, observed doubles over the number expected under independence, and interference, one minus coincidence.
cards.section: Compare observed doubles with chance

cards.front: Interference equals {{c1::one minus the coefficient of coincidence}}.
cards.quote: coefficient of coincidence, observed doubles over the number expected under independence, and interference, one minus coincidence.
cards.section: Compare observed doubles with chance

cards.front: Adjacent intervals have recombination fractions 0.10 and 0.20, and 1,000 progeny show 5 doubles. What are the expected doubles, the coincidence and the interference?
cards.back: Expected = 0.10 × 0.20 × 1,000 = 20. Coincidence = 5/20 = 0.25. Interference = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75: fewer doubles than chance predicts.
cards.quote: expected doubles = 0.12 × 0.20 × 1,000 = 24 coincidence = 12 / 24 = 0.50 interference = 1 − 0.50 = 0.50
cards.section: Compare observed doubles with chance

cards.front: In an X–Y–Z cross with intervals 0.176 and 0.206, 1,000 progeny and 16 observed doubles, what are the expected doubles, the coincidence and the interference?
cards.back: Expected = 0.176 × 0.206 × 1,000 = about 36.3. Coincidence = 16/36.3 = about 0.44. Interference = about 0.56, positive.
cards.quote: expected doubles = 0.12 × 0.20 × 1,000 = 24 coincidence = 12 / 24 = 0.50 interference = 1 − 0.50 = 0.50
cards.section: Compare observed doubles with chance

cards.front: What does positive interference mean?
cards.back: A crossover in one interval is associated with fewer crossovers in the neighbouring interval, so observed doubles fall below the number expected under independence.
cards.quote: This is positive interference: a crossover in one interval is associated with fewer crossovers in the neighbouring interval.
cards.section: Compare observed doubles with chance

cards.front: What do an interference of 1 and a coincidence above 1 each mean?
cards.back: Interference of 1 means no doubles at all. A coincidence above 1 is negative interference, an excess of doubles, which is not impossible.
cards.quote: Interference of 1 means no doubles at all; a coincidence above 1 is negative interference, an excess of doubles, not an impossible result.
cards.section: Compare observed doubles with chance

cards.front: Two short adjacent intervals each give 3% recombinants in a cross of 10,000 progeny, and 15 progeny are recombinant in both. What is the interference, and what does its sign mean?
cards.back: Expected = 0.03 × 0.03 × 10,000 = 9. Coincidence = 15/9 = 1.67; interference = −0.67. Negative interference: more doubles than independence predicts.
cards.quote: Interference of 1 means no doubles at all; a coincidence above 1 is negative interference, an excess of doubles, not an impossible result.
cards.section: Compare observed doubles with chance

cards.front: Why is interference a property of one pair of intervals in one organism, not a species constant? Where is it strongest?
cards.back: It tends to be strongest across short neighbouring intervals, and for intervals far apart, coincidence approaches 1 (no interference).
cards.quote: interference tends to be strongest across short neighbouring intervals, and for intervals far apart, coincidence approaches 1.
cards.section: Compare observed doubles with chance

cards.front: A three-point cross has 500 progeny and intervals of 6 cM and 10 cM, and no doubles appear. Does that prove complete interference?
cards.back: No. Independence predicts 0.06 × 0.10 × 500 = 3 doubles, so P(0) = e^-3, about 0.05, even with no interference. Zero is suggestive but cannot distinguish complete interference from interference of 0.5.
cards.why: Rests on the independent expectation as a Poisson mean.
cards.quote: So even without interference, about one cross in twenty this size shows zero doubles.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: For the 6 cM and 10 cM cross, how does scoring 5,000 progeny instead of 500 change what zero doubles would show?
cards.back: Independence now predicts 30 doubles, so P(0) is about 10^-13. Zero doubles would mean interference near complete; about 15 doubles would mean interference near 0.5.
cards.quote: With 5,000, independence predicts 30 doubles and P(0) = e^-30, about 10^-13.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: In humans and mice, where do most crossovers fall?
cards.back: In hotspots: short DNA stretches with much more recombination than the DNA around them.
cards.quote: In humans and mice, most crossovers fall in hotspots, short DNA stretches with much more recombination than the DNA around them.
cards.section: Genetic distance is not DNA length

cards.front: Two human marker pairs lie 1 million base pairs apart, one 0.2 cM apart and the other 3 cM. What best explains the difference, and what does it show about cM and DNA length?
cards.back: The 3 cM pair likely spans more crossover hotspots. A centimorgan is a recombination frequency, not a fixed length of DNA.
cards.quote: In humans the genome-wide average is close to 1 cM per million base pairs, only a rough average.
cards.section: Genetic distance is not DNA length

cards.front: What does the PRDM9 protein do in human and mouse recombination?
cards.back: It binds particular DNA sequences through its zinc fingers and marks nearby sites where recombination starts.
cards.quote: whose protein binds particular DNA sequences through zinc fingers and marks nearby sites where recombination starts
cards.section: Genetic distance is not DNA length

cards.front: In humans or mice, if the zinc-finger array of PRDM9 changes, should the same DNA sites remain hotspots?
cards.back: Not necessarily: the bound sequences change, so hotspots move. People with different zinc-finger variants used different hotspots across the genome.
cards.quote: Not necessarily: the bound sequences change, so hotspots move.
cards.section: Genetic distance is not DNA length

cards.front: Dogs lack working PRDM9. Predict where their hotspots lie, and what this shows about PRDM9.
cards.back: Hotspots tend to lie near promoter-like features such as transcription start sites and CpG islands. So PRDM9 is not the only way animals place hotspots.
cards.quote: Dogs lack working PRDM9, birds appear to lack the gene, and their hotspots tend to lie near promoter-like features such as transcription start sites and CpG islands.
cards.section: Genetic distance is not DNA length

cards.front: How does the human female genetic map compare with the male map across the genome?
cards.back: The female map is about 1.6 to 1.7 times the male map.
cards.quote: Across the genome, the human female map is about 1.6 to 1.7 times the male map.
cards.section: Genetic distance is not DNA length

cards.front: Why do Drosophila melanogaster mapping crosses use a triple-heterozygous female rather than a male?
cards.back: D. melanogaster males normally have no meiotic crossing over, so only the female's gametes can show recombination.
cards.quote: Drosophila melanogaster males normally have no meiotic crossing over, although males of some species, including D. ananassae, do.
cards.section: Genetic distance is not DNA length

cards.front: Where is crossing over suppressed in many organisms, including Drosophila and Arabidopsis?
cards.back: Near centromeres.
cards.quote: Crossovers are suppressed near centromeres in many organisms, including Drosophila and Arabidopsis
cards.section: Genetic distance is not DNA length

cards.front: A female fly heterozygous at D, E and F is test-crossed to a recessive male. Of 1,000 progeny, the largest classes are d E f (412) and D e F (405); the smallest are d E F (6) and D e f (8). What is the gene order, and why?
cards.back: d–f–e: F is in the middle. Each rare class differs from its closest parental only at F, so F is the gene that switches in the doubles.
cards.quote: So p is in the middle, giving q–p–r.
cards.section: Read the eight classes in a fixed order

cards.front: A genetic map and the genome sequence of the same region disagree on the spacing of three genes but agree on order. What is each best used for?
cards.back: Use the genetic map to predict how often genes travel together, and the sequence to measure how much DNA separates them.
cards.quote: Use a genetic map to predict how often genes travel together; use sequence to measure how much DNA separates them.
cards.section: Genetic distance is not DNA length

cards.front: Is positive interference universal?
cards.back: No. It is common, but negative interference has been reported in some fungal and phage crosses.
cards.quote: Positive interference is common, but not universal.
cards.section: Going deeper: when the simple comparison changes
